text:
Every recovery schedule I have reviewed had one thing in common: the end date did not move.

The project is three months late. A recovery schedule is requested. Two weeks later it arrives, and the completion date is exactly where it was in the baseline.

How? Almost always the same way:
• durations cut by 30 % with no change in crews or method
• activities that were sequential now run in parallel, on the same piece of steel
• productivity assumed at a rate the site has never achieved, not even for one week

On paper the gap is closed. On site, somebody has to close it, and that somebody is a person.

A recovery nobody resourced is paid for in 12-hour days, cancelled leave and weekends on site. Construction research from five countries says what that costs:
• UK: 94 % of construction professionals felt stress in the past year, and 24 % felt it every day. The causes they named most were too much work and unrealistic deadlines (CIOB, 2025).
• US: 64 % of construction workers had anxiety or depression in the past year, up from 54 % a year earlier. Project deadlines were among the main causes (Clayco, 2025).
• South Africa: for engineers, quantity surveyors and construction managers, tight deadlines and long hours mattered more to stress than how much control they had over the job (Bowen et al., 2013).
• Australia: on a major project, weekly hours rose sharply before each milestone, leaving people less time to recover (Lingard et al., 2010).
• Saudi Arabia: on 16 construction sites, stress helped predict who got injured (2025 study of 349 workers).

Five countries, and the same cause keeps coming back: the deadline. I could not find one published figure for construction in the UAE. Maybe it is time someone asked us.

So the unrealistic schedule fails twice. It misses the date, and it wears out the people we need to finish the job.

A real recovery plan answers five questions:
1. What is different from now on: crews, shifts, sequence, method?
2. Can the site absorb it: supervision, access, permits, cranes?
3. What productivity does it need, and when did we last achieve it?
4. What does it ask of the people, and for how long?
5. If it still does not close the gap, what is the honest date?

If you work on a site in the UAE: when a recovery schedule is signed, who counts the hours it will take from the team? And what did the last "recovered" date really cost the people on your project?

#ProjectControls #Planning #Wellbeing #Construction #Leadership

A Gantt chart compares the current forecast, three months late, with a 'recovery' schedule that reaches the contract end date by cutting piping durations 30 % with the same crews and running hydrotest in parallel on the same steel. The people who must deliver it, from construction studies: 94 % of construction professionals felt stress in the past year (CIOB, 2025, UK, 865 surveyed); 64 % of construction workers had anxiety or depression in the past year (Clayco, 2025, US); too much work and unrealistic deadlines were the causes named most (CIOB, 2025). A real recovery also answers: what does it ask of the people, and for how long? And what is the honest date?
